rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to locate the elution window and critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A moderate temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Change only gradient duration to measure whether the critical cluster responds to a shallower slope. The last peak should remain near or below 10 minutes, leaving time to improve resolution without a substantial time penalty.

Raise the starting organic fraction to trim the weak-solvent portion of the gradient while making its slope shallower. This should improve the slope-sensitive critical pair and keep the last peak below 10 minutes; the first peak should still be retained.
Lengthen the gradient by one grid step to improve the remaining critical pair. Based on the observed slope response, this may reach R ≥ 1.5 while keeping the last peak just below 10 minutes.

The maximum CRF is already achieved, so test a 5 °C temperature increase to shorten elution while preserving full resolution. Keeping the gradient unchanged isolates temperature selectivity at the critical pair.

The critical pair converged sharply at 45 °C; testing 55 °C may separate it again after an elution-order reversal while shortening retention. Keep the gradient fixed to assess temperature selectivity and check for new critical pairs.

Lengthen the gradient one step to improve the newly limiting pair at 55 °C. The last peak is expected to remain below 10 minutes, so this tests a second fully resolved operating region without an anticipated time penalty.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step to shorten the fully resolved 55 °C method while slightly reducing gradient steepness. Check both critical pairs and the early peaks, which may become less retained.

Lowering phi0 should improve the early separation and the pair that deteriorated at phi0 0.20. Combine this with a shorter gradient to seek full resolution at a shorter last-peak time, while checking the other temperature-sensitive pair.
Shorten the fastest fully resolved method by one gradient-duration step. This tests whether both critical pairs retain R ≥ 1.5 as the last-peak time decreases.

Lower phi1 to obtain a slope between the 12- and 14-minute gradients already tested, aiming to restore full resolution with an earlier last peak than injection 9. The observed elution window suggests all compounds will still elute during the gradient.

Use a slightly steeper slope than injection 11 to shorten retention while targeting full resolution of both critical pairs. The final organic fraction remains comfortably above the estimated last-peak elution fraction, so all peaks should remain inside the gradient.

Test a faster, hotter gradient for a new selectivity region where the current limiting pair may reverse order and separate again. This exploratory run could substantially shorten elution; injection 12 remains the fastest fully resolved fallback.

Raise phi0 one step to test whether the selectivity shift seen at higher starting organic now separates the reversed critical pair at 60 °C. This should also shorten retention, while the early pair is expected to remain sufficiently retained and resolved.

Explore the low-temperature selectivity region with a short gradient, since the high-temperature fast methods retain a limiting pair. Temperature-driven order changes may enable a faster fully resolved method; the strong endpoint should keep all compounds observable.

Return to the successful 55 °C region and lower phi0 relative to injection 10 to improve its limiting pair. This may achieve full resolution with a last-peak time shorter than injection 12, though the other close pair must be checked.

Compare with injection 14 to measure the slope response of the reversed critical pair at 60 °C. A longer gradient should improve the neighboring separation and reveal whether this hotter region can support full resolution faster than injection 16.

Test a modestly steeper gradient than injection 16 to locate the shortest fully resolved boundary at 55 °C. Both critical pairs are close to the threshold, so this is a deliberate boundary test with injection 16 retained as the fallback.

Test an intermediate low-temperature selectivity region using the same gradient as injection 16. This checks whether cooling separates the central cluster sufficiently to permit further shortening, while retaining the established maximum-CRF methods as fallbacks.

Test whether a steep gradient at 45 °C separates the central cluster after an order reversal, offering a substantially faster alternative. The low starting organic fraction protects early retention; injection 16 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Refine the established fully resolved 40 °C method by raising phi0 one step to shorten retention. This tests whether its critical pair remains resolved without compressing the early pair below R = 1.5.

Trim injection 16’s gradient endpoint while preserving its successful slope of 0.075 organic fraction per minute. The last peak is expected before the gradient ends at the outlet, so this should preserve maximum CRF with a shorter programmed gradient and lower organic consumption.

Test whether a low starting organic fraction and shallower gradient restore separation beyond the critical-pair crossover at 60 °C. The last peak is expected below 10 minutes, allowing a potentially fully resolved alternative with greater separation of the other central pair.

Refine the fully resolved region around injection 7 with a slightly shallower slope and a trimmed endpoint. This should preserve maximum CRF with more resolution margin than the fastest methods, while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.

Use a slope between injections 6 and 7 to target full resolution with a last peak near 9 minutes and more separation margin than the fastest methods. Injection 22 remains the shortest-gradient confirmed method achieving maximum CRF.
